questions.text: What is the "controller" that resumes after a restart, and what does it actually do versus what a person does? Who checks that a gate is met before a person approves?
questions.about: Where the rollout state lives / Forward moves are one step at a time and each one is made by a person

questions.text: When someone sets billing_mode, how do the old and new engines learn about it? Do they read the config service on every run, or is it pushed to them?
questions.about: The mode: single global billing_mode flag in the config service

questions.text: In shadow, what exactly does the nightly job compare, and where does it read each engine's invoice from? What counts toward the 5000 invoices compared?
questions.about: shadow --> both gate; Modes: shadow

questions.text: What measures the new-engine charge failure rate, and what counts as a failure (declined card, provider error, timeout)? Who or what triggers the automatic rollback when the 2 percent is crossed?
questions.about: Automatic rollback: failure rate above 2 percent in any 10 min window

questions.text: In RB1, how do you stop new-engine charging, and what happens to a charge already sent to the provider? How is it resolved by the idempotency key?
questions.about: rb_freeze --> rb_catch_up: in-flight charges resolved by provider idempotency key

questions.text: In RB2, what does reconcile compare, and what does it mean for it to fail? Who is notified when it enters rb_stalled?
questions.about: rb_catch_up --> rb_stalled: reconcile fails

questions.text: In RB3, how does the old engine decide an invoice is due and not yet charged? Which invoices were already charged by the new engine and so must be skipped?
questions.about: rb_cutover --> old_only: due uncharged invoices charged once

questions.text: In both mode the old engine writes to the shadow store while the new engine writes the ledger. Which invoices does the customer actually receive, and what is the ledger's role versus the provider's?
questions.about: Modes: both; Other stores: shadow store separate from the ledger

answers.text: The controller is not written yet. This file defines it as the component that keeps the rollout record, counts gate days and refuses a forward move until its gate is met. A person makes and approves each forward move; the controller only checks the gate and never moves the mode forward. Reason: the brief says a person always makes forward moves, and a code check stops an approval made before a gate is met.
The brief does not say whether the engines read billing_mode on every run or receive it pushed. Listed under open questions.

Per the brief, the old engine's invoices are in the ledger and the new engine's invoices are in the shadow store, so the nightly job compares those two sources per customer. The brief does not say whether the 5,000 counts invoices or customer and billing period pairs; that is listed as an open question.

The brief does not say how the 2 percent charge failure rate is measured or which outcomes count as failures, including declines versus provider errors and timeouts. Listed under open questions, with the risk that declines could trigger rollback.

RB1 stops new-engine charging, so no new charge is sent; how the freeze is switched off is not in the brief and is listed as open. A charge already sent is not sent again. Its status is looked up at the provider by its idempotency key (customer, billing period, invoice). Reason: this is how the never-charge-twice rule holds when a charge's status is unknown.

Reconcile compares, per customer and billing period, the ledger, the provider's status for each idempotency key, and the old engine's recomputed invoices. It fails if any difference remains. Reason: these three records must agree before the old engine charges again. Who is notified on rb_stalled is not in the brief and is listed as open.

An invoice is due and uncharged if neither the ledger nor the provider shows a successful charge under its idempotency key. The same check skips invoices the new engine already charged. Reason: the key is per customer, period and invoice, so this check identifies a charge reliably.

In both mode the new engine charges and writes the ledger, so the customer receives the new engine's invoices (per the brief). The ledger is the system of record for what was billed; the provider holds payment status. The shadow store holds the old engine's invoices for comparison and is never customer-facing.

questions.text: In both, the new engine writes the ledger and the old engine writes the shadow store. Does the nightly job still compare the same two sources, with the roles swapped? Which side counts as correct when they differ?
questions.about: Modes: both (nightly comparison continues)

questions.text: What does it mean for a mismatch to be resolved, and who resolves it? Does a new mismatch in both reset the 14-day count the way it resets the 7-day streak in shadow?
questions.about: both --> new_only gate: no unresolved mismatches

questions.text: What makes the move to retired happen on day 35? Is it automatic, or does a person do it? Who actually decommissions the old engine?
questions.about: new_only --> retired: day 35 in new_only

questions.text: What moves the rollback from RB1 to RB2? Is it when every in-flight charge has a known status? What happens if the provider is slow or does not answer for a charge?
questions.about: rb_freeze --> rb_catch_up: in-flight charges resolved by provider idempotency key

questions.text: While the rollback is frozen or stalled, nobody charges customers. Is there a limit on how long this can last, and what happens to customers' invoices that come due in the meantime?
questions.about: Rollback stalled: Due charges are delayed, not dropped

questions.text: After the automatic rollback starts, who is told, and does on-call have to do anything for RB2 and RB3 to run? Or do they run on their own?
questions.about: Automatic rollback: both --> rb_freeze

questions.text: What happens if the failure rate goes above 2 percent after day 35, in retired? Is there any rollback or other response then?
questions.about: Rollback: on-call rollback before day 35

answers.text: The comparison continues with the sources swapped. In both, the new engine's invoices are in the ledger and the old engine's are in the shadow store, so the nightly job compares ledger to shadow store per customer. The brief names the ledger as system of record, so it is the reference for what was billed. The brief does not say which engine is right when they differ, so the file does not let either engine override the other: a mismatch goes to a person and nothing is corrected automatically. Reason: that keeps the never-charge-twice and record rules without trusting either engine by default.

The brief says no unresolved mismatches, but does not define resolved, who resolves a mismatch, or whether a new mismatch restarts the 14-day count. The file now states only that the gate needs no open mismatch when a person approves. This is listed under open questions.

Not automatic. The brief says the old engine may be decommissioned after 35 days in new_only, which gives a person a choice rather than a required step. The rollback window closes on day 35 by itself, because the skipped events age out of the log. Who performs the decommission is not in the brief and is listed as open.

RB1 moves to RB2 when every in-flight charge has a known status at the provider. If the provider is slow or does not answer for a charge, that charge stays unknown, its lookup is repeated, and the rollback stays in RB1 with new charging still frozen. Reason: RB3 charges invoices that have no successful charge, so moving on with an unknown status could send a second charge, which the never-charge-twice rule forbids. The brief sets no time limit for this wait (see Q13).

The brief sets no time limit on a freeze or a stall, and it says due charges must not be dropped. The file treats them as delayed: invoices that come due are charged once in RB3, after reconciliation. The only hard limit in the brief is the 35-day usage event log. A rollback from new_only needs the skipped events, and they age out at day 35, so a stall past day 35 leaves the old engine unable to recompute them. Escalation and who is told are open.

The brief says the controller starts RB1 on its own. It does not say who is told when that happens, or whether RB2 and RB3 run without a person. The file does not decide this. It is listed under open questions.

No rollback. The brief says there is no way back from day 35, and retired has no transition to old_only. The 2 percent automatic rule applies only in both and new_only, so it has no effect in retired. What on-call should do about new-engine failures in retired is not in the brief and is listed as open.

questions.text: When the new engine charges in 'both', what exactly starts that charge, and what does it write to the ledger and when? I need the order: charge sent, provider answers, ledger written.
questions.about: Modes: both

questions.text: The text says a charge can succeed but the ledger write fail, or the reverse. Who or what notices that, and does it happen as a routine check or only during rollback?
questions.about: What happens when something fails: Charge succeeded but ledger write failed

questions.text: In rollback from new_only, the old engine recomputes skipped usage events. Where does it read them from, and where do the new engine's invoices for that period go, given the new engine wrote the ledger?
questions.about: RB2 reconcile and catch up

questions.text: In RB3, when the old engine charges an invoice, where does it write the result? Does it write the ledger, and what happens to the ledger entries the new engine wrote?
questions.about: RB3 cutover

questions.text: Who sets billing_mode to shadow at the start, and how does the controller know a person has 'approved'? Is approval a button, a command, or a config change?
questions.about: A person makes each forward move

questions.text: What does on-call do to start a rollback by hand, and does the controller refuse it after day 35 or does on-call just have to know?
questions.about: On-call starts a rollback by hand within the 35-day limit

questions.text: During RB1 to RB3 the mode is still both or new_only. What do customers and the engines see during that time, and does billing_mode change when RB1 starts?
questions.about: Rollback (RB1 to RB3)

answers.text: The new engine sends one charge for each invoice that is due, keyed on customer, billing period and invoice. The provider answers. Only after that does the new engine write the invoice and the charge result to the ledger. Reason: the brief's failure case (charge succeeded, ledger write failed) only makes sense if the charge comes first, and the idempotency key has to exist before the charge is sent. The brief does not say what starts a charge run, so that is listed as open, not decided here.

The brief does not say whether a charge that succeeded with a failed ledger write is noticed by a routine check or only during rollback. The file's rule is the provider lookup by key, which applies either way. Detection is listed under open questions.

The old engine reads the skipped usage events from the usage event log, which keeps 35 days (per the brief). Its recomputed invoices go to the shadow store, not the ledger (per RB2 in the file). The new engine's invoices stay in the ledger. Reconcile then compares the ledger, the provider's status and the shadow store. The file now names both sources in RB2.

The old engine writes each invoice and charge result it creates to the ledger, as it does in old_only. It does not edit or delete the rows the new engine wrote, because the ledger is the record of what was billed. RB3 skips any invoice with a successful charge, so the new engine's charged invoices are not charged again. Any remaining difference goes to a person through reconcile. Reason: no engine overwrites another engine's record.

The brief says a person makes forward moves, but not how the change is made or how approval is recorded. Whether approval is a button, a command or a config change is not in the brief. The file also has a gap: it says the controller refuses a forward move, but nothing stops someone from setting billing_mode directly. Both are listed under open questions.

The brief does not say how on-call starts a rollback by hand, so that is open. The brief does say the 35-day limit applies to the hand start. The controller therefore refuses a rollback from new_only that starts after day 35, because the skipped events have aged out and RB2 cannot run. The controller counts the days, so on-call does not need to know the date. Reason: the brief calls day 35 the point with no way back.

billing_mode does not change when RB1 starts. It stays both or new_only until RB3 finishes, then becomes old_only. Reason: the brief says a rollback always ends in old_only and sets no intermediate mode. The rollback step lives in the rollout record. Customers get no new charges during RB1 and RB2, and due invoices wait until RB3 charges each one once. The new engine is frozen in RB1, and the old engine computes without charging in RB2. Whether an engine that reads only billing_mode would keep charging during RB1 depends on the freeze mechanism, which is open.

teachbacks.text:
1. The system has one global setting, `billing_mode`, kept in the config service. It has four values: old_only, shadow, both, new_only. Every rollout starts in old_only. In that mode the old engine reads usage events, computes invoices, writes the ledger and charges customers. The new engine is off.

2. A person sets `billing_mode` to shadow. The old engine keeps charging and writing the ledger. The new engine now reads the same usage events and writes its invoices to a separate shadow store. It never charges and never writes the ledger.

3. A nightly job compares, per customer, the old engine's invoices (read from the ledger) with the new engine's (read from the shadow store). An invoice is a mismatch if the totals differ by more than one cent. The rollout controller counts the days and shows whether the gate is met. The controller is "not written yet".

4. If a day's mismatch rate is at or above 0.1 percent, the 7-day streak restarts. Nothing else happens and the mode stays put. Errors from the new engine in shadow are recorded but never cause a rollback.

5. The gate for moving from shadow to both is 7 consecutive days below 0.1 percent mismatch and at least 5000 invoices compared. The controller refuses the move until the gate is met. When it is met, a person approves and makes the move. Nothing moves forward on its own.

6. In both, the new engine charges and writes the ledger. For each invoice that is due, the new engine sends one charge to the provider, keyed on customer, billing period and invoice. The provider answers. Only after that does the new engine write the invoice and the charge result to the ledger. The old engine keeps computing every invoice into the shadow store without charging, so it can take over. The nightly comparison now runs the other way: the ledger (new engine) against the shadow store (old engine). The ledger is the reference. A mismatch goes to a person and nothing is corrected automatically.

7. The gate for both to new_only is 14 days in both, no open mismatch and Finance sign-off. A person approves, and the controller enforces the gate. In new_only the new engine does everything. The old engine stops computing, so usage events are skipped from then on. The usage event log keeps only 35 days of events.

8. After 35 days in new_only, rollback is closed because the skipped events have aged out. A person may then decide to decommission the old engine. That moves the system to retired, which has no way back.

9. Rollback can start in two ways. On-call can start it by hand from shadow, both, or new_only (new_only only before day 35). Alternatively, in both or new_only, the controller starts it on its own when the new-engine charge failure rate is above 2 percent in any 10-minute window.

10. Rollback from shadow is only a flag change back to old_only, because the old engine has charged all along.

11. Rollback from both or new_only runs three steps, and the current step is kept in the rollout record. `billing_mode` does not change until RB3 finishes.

12. RB1 freeze. The new engine stops sending new charges. A charge already sent is never re-sent. For each in-flight charge, the system asks the provider for its status using the idempotency key. A charge whose status is still unknown is looked up again. RB1 ends only when every in-flight charge has a known status. This matters because RB3 charges any invoice without a successful charge, so an unknown charge could be charged twice.

13. RB2 reconcile and catch up. The old engine reads the skipped usage events from the usage event log and recomputes them into the shadow store, with no charges. Reconcile then compares, per customer and billing period, three things: the ledger (new engine's invoices), the provider's status for each key, and the shadow store (old engine's recomputed invoices). If any difference remains, reconcile fails.

14. If reconcile fails, the rollback enters rb_stalled. New-engine charging stays frozen. The old engine does not charge. Due invoices are delayed, not dropped. On-call escalates. There are two ways out. If the cause is fixed, the rollback resumes at RB2. Alternatively, a signed-off manual reconciliation per invoice sends it straight to RB3. The document gives no time limit.

15. RB3 cutover. The old engine charges only invoices that are due and have no successful charge. An invoice counts as having one if the ledger or the provider shows a charge under its key, so invoices the new engine already charged are skipped. The old engine writes each invoice and charge result to the ledger and does not change ledger rows the new engine wrote. Then `billing_mode` is set to old_only and all gates reset.

16. After a rollback the system is in old_only. Going back to shadow needs a person, and the 7-day count starts over.

17. Charge/ledger failure. If a charge succeeded but the ledger write failed, or the reverse, the fix is to query the provider with the idempotency key before charging anything again. The system never re-charges on an unknown status.

18. State summary. The mode lives in `billing_mode` in the config service. The ledger is the record of what was billed. The provider holds payment status. The shadow store is separate and never customer-facing. The streak counters, Finance sign-off, new_only day count and current rollback step are not specified. The document only recommends putting them in one rollout record next to `billing_mode`.
gaps: How the engines learn the value of billing_mode: whether they read it on every run or it is pushed. Without this I cannot say how a mode change reaches the engines.
What starts a charge run in both: a schedule or an event. I can't explain what triggers step 6.
How the new engine's charge path is switched off in RB1, and whether the flag alone is enough. billing_mode does not change until RB3, so the stop mechanism is unexplained.
How a forward move is enforced and approval recorded: whether someone could set billing_mode directly and skip the gate, and who records approval and the Finance sign-off.
How on-call starts a rollback by hand.
How the 2 percent failure rate is measured and whether card declines count as failures.

What counts toward the 5000 invoices, whether the 0.1 percent applies per day or to the whole window, and what 'resolved' means for a mismatch in both (who resolves it, and whether a new one restarts the 14-day count).
Where the streak counters, new_only day count and rollback step are actually stored. The document recommends a rollout record but leaves it as an open decision.
Whether RB2 and RB3 run without a person, and who is notified when an automatic rollback starts or when rb_stalled is entered.
Who notices a charge whose ledger write failed outside a rollback, and how.
Whether the 35-day clock counts from entry into new_only. The document says the brief does not say.
Who decommissions the old engine, and what happens on new-engine failures once the system is in retired.
